text: Cold open.
On Saturday, October 17th, Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy announced that the Strait of Hormuz is closed, and that passage is prohibited.
That's according to Iran's state news agency, IRNA.
The day before, the head of US Central Command had said something quite different.

In a video message, Admiral Brad Cooper said the strait is "controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran." He said about four hundred merchant ships had crossed in the previous seven days.
One narrow waterway.
Two official statements.
And then there are the independent trackers, which are counting something else again: anywhere from single digits to a dozen or so ships a day.
On October 18th, the maritime-intelligence firm Windward counted twelve, four of them with their tracking signals off.
So how can a strait be closed and open at the same time?
Here's the short answer.
"Closed" isn't one thing.
There's closed by law.
Closed by weapons.
Closed by insurance.
Closed by permission.
Closed by fear.
And those don't always move together.
This video is not about who is right.
It's about how it works: the mechanisms that decide whether a strait is open, closed, or somewhere in between.
One rule before we start.
Every number you'll hear is attributed to a named source, and all of them are listed in the description.
Where sources disagree, you'll hear both.
Part one.
The Stakes.
The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
At its narrowest, it's only about 35 to 40 kilometers wide.
The International Energy Agency says about a quarter of the world's seaborne oil trade, and about 20 percent of its liquefied natural gas, moved through it in 2025.
Before the war began on February 28th, the agency puts the oil flow at around 20 million barrels a day.
The IEA calls what followed the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.
In its October report, published on October 14th, the agency estimated that oil flows through the strait recovered in September to about 10.9 million barrels a day.
That's up by 3.7 million from August, but still only a little over half of the pre-war level.
That is why the story matters far beyond the Gulf: fuel and shipping costs everywhere are exposed to it.
Part two.
Two Statements.
Let's start with exactly what each side is saying.
Iran.
The Revolutionary Guards Navy statement, carried by IRNA, said the strait is closed and passage is prohibited.
It warned ships against violating Iranian regulations.
The Guards' spokesman, Mohebbi, has said that an open strait should see about 125 ships and 20 million barrels a day passing through.
Those levels are not being met, he says, so the strait is closed.
This was not the first such announcement.
The Joint Maritime Information Center, known as JMIC, which is run by the 47-nation Combined Maritime Forces, recorded an Iranian proclamation that the strait was closed on July 12th as well.
Its advisories include figures supplied by US forces.
The Guards themselves described the October 17th statement as another declaration.
The United States.

On October 17th, Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesman for US Central Command, said the strait is open and available for transit, and that about 97 percent of the ships that sought to cross have done so successfully.
The day before, CENTCOM's commander, Admiral Brad Cooper, said the strait is controlled by the United States and its regional partners, not Iran.
He said about 400 merchant ships had crossed in the previous seven days, and that US forces had helped Gulf partners ship more than 100 million barrels of crude in that same week.
Two details about the reporting.
In the coverage used here, the 97 percent figure came without a time window or a ship count, and Cooper's seven days were not broken down day by day.
And the Guards' 125-ship threshold is their own definition of "open." Now, one way to read all this.
It's this video's reading, not either side's.
Iran is describing "open" as normal: normal traffic, normal volumes, no interference.
The US is describing "open" as ships getting through.
Part of the gap is definitional.
But the statements also make competing claims about who controls the strait, and that reading doesn't settle those.
Part three.
The Counting Problem.
So what's actually happening on the water?
This is where it gets complicated, because the numbers themselves disagree.
First: what's normal?
It depends on the dataset.
The International Monetary Fund's PortWatch, as cited by the economics publication EconoFact, showed an average of about 103 trading-ship arrivals a day in the week before the war.
Reuters reports about 125 large commercial vessels a day. gCaptain cites a 2025 average of about 138.
And some tracker sites cite figures closer to 85, depending on which ships they count.
Second: what's happening now?
Kpler counted seven commodity vessels on October 6th, not counting ships with their transponders off.
Reuters reported that as the lowest since July 23rd.

In its October 15th advisory, marked as a draft, JMIC reported single-digit daily numbers for October 8th to 14th, from independent data on cargo ships and tankers that excludes vessels calling at nearby Iranian ports.
And Windward's own page showed twelve crossings on October 18th, five inbound and seven outbound, four of them with their transponders off.
Windward also cautions that counts of dark transits can't always be compared across dates, because its detection coverage has changed.
Third: the US count.
The same advisory cites US Navy shipping-guidance data showing 121 US-facilitated transits between October 11th and 14th.
That's about 30 a day.

Then comes one of the most detailed documents available: the weekly overview from UKMTO, the UK Maritime Trade Operations center, which describes itself as a neutral and impartial information provider.
In its report dated October 16th, covering data through October 14th, UKMTO recorded 254 combined transits, about 70 percent below pre-war levels.
But look inside that number.
Only 42 were observed through AIS, the ship-tracking signal.
UKMTO adds that the US-stated facilitated transits are a separate dataset, which it says it can't independently verify.
It calls the two sets "related but distinct." So why can't anyone simply count?
Because of AIS.
Ships are supposed to broadcast their position.
But in this part of the world, many don't, and JMIC reports that ships broadcasting AIS face a higher risk of being targeted.
Other signals are distorted: UKMTO logged more than 23,000 anomalous AIS positions in a single week, in areas where it also received reports of satellite-navigation interference.
This video doesn't attribute that to anyone.
In one snapshot on May 8th, Windward detected 521 radio transmissions around Hormuz, and only 84 matched an AIS broadcast.

In early September, Drewry analyst Eirik Hooper told Al Jazeera that a US operational count "plausibly includes" everything that moved under or near naval protection, including support ships, tugs and small coastal boats.
That is his inference, a hypothesis, not a finding, and none of the other sources used in this video confirms it.
So here's the honest takeaway.
When you see a number about Hormuz, ask three questions.
Which ships are counted?
Over what window?
And how does the source know?
Part four.
Seven Levers.
A strait isn't a door.
It doesn't close with one handle.
This video sorts the mechanisms into seven levers.
Some sit with governments, and some don't.
Lever one.
Law And Declaration..
Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, ships have a right of "transit passage" through straits like Hormuz, and coastal states may not suspend it.
Iran has not ratified that convention, and neither has the United States.
Reuters reports that experts generally treat the core rules as customary international law, while Iran argues it has consistently objected to them.
In a July advisory, JMIC said the strait is not subject to coercion or control by any single nation.
Iran says its restrictions are national security and self-defense measures in wartime.
A declaration, by itself, doesn't stop a single ship.
What it does is change what happens if one tries.
Lever two.
Weapons..
In this video's judgment, this is the lever with the most immediate effect.
UKMTO recorded 12 attacks in its latest weekly report, ten of them in the strait.
JMIC counts 149 confirmed vessel incidents across the wider region since March 1st, and rates the threat level in the strait as "severe", the second-highest on its scale.
The International Maritime Organization's list of highlighted incidents shows 24 seafarer deaths as of October 14th.
Who is responsible is often left unstated in the reports themselves.
UKMTO's incident entries mostly say "unknown projectile." CENTCOM says the container ship GFS Pride was hit by a projectile from Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
The Guards said it struck a mine, on a route Iran says was unauthorized.
JMIC said there was no substantiation for the mine claim.
One more detail: UKMTO says 55 of the 74 projectile strikes since July 6th hit ships on the southern route, the lane where US-assisted transits take place.
This video draws no conclusion from that.
Lever three.
Mines..
A mine doesn't need to hit anything to close a strait.
The suspicion is enough.
In 1987, the supertanker Bridgeton struck a mine during the first US-escorted convoy of Operation Earnest Will.
In late August, Admiral Cooper said US forces had cleared the main shipping lanes of mines.
Bloomberg reported that some allies privately doubted it.
JMIC's advisories continue to warn of possible mining in and around the traditional shipping lanes.
On October 17th, Iran's Guards said two tankers hit mines after trying a route Iran hadn't authorized.
State media put the cargo at about two million barrels of crude.
Reuters noted there was no independent confirmation.
It wasn't the first such claim.
At the end of August, Iran's Guards said a large tanker on the southern route had hit two mines.
US Central Command answered that no ship was struck by mines and called the claim false.
Neither side offered evidence in the reporting used here.
So here is what's on the record.
Iran says mines.
The US says the main lanes are clear.
And nobody independent has confirmed the October 17th incidents.
Lever four.
Insurance..
Ships can't sail without it.
Early in the war, the Lloyd's Market Association pushed back on the idea that cover had disappeared.
War insurance remained available, it said.
In its view, ships were held back because masters and owners judged the risk to crew and vessel too high.
But the price moved.
Before the war, war-risk premiums were around a quarter of one percent of a ship's value, according to The National.
By July, a Marsh executive told S&P Global that additional war-risk premiums had reached 7.5 to 10 percent of hull value.
On a 100-million-dollar tanker, that works out to between 7.5 and 10 million dollars.
Those are July figures.
Rates are repriced constantly, so treat them as a snapshot, not today's price.
Lever five.
Permits And Fees..
Since May, Iran has run a permit system through a body it calls the Persian Gulf Strait Authority.
Ships submit an application by email and are directed to a route near Iran's coast.
In March, an Iranian lawmaker said on state television that some ships were being charged two million dollars.
The sources used here carry no independent confirmation of that figure.
The US Treasury sanctioned that authority on May 27th, called its tolls illegitimate, and warned that anyone cooperating could face sanctions risk.
In July, President Trump announced that the US would charge a 20 percent fee on cargo passing through the strait, though the sources used here give no details on how it would work.
And JMIC, in a July advisory, said there is no controlling authority regulating passage and no fee required for any route.
So a shipowner faces two rival sets of rules, and a different kind of risk with each.
Lever six.
Visibility..
This one is almost invisible.
According to JMIC, ships that broadcast AIS face a higher risk of being targeted, and are hailed with instructions to divert to Iran's northern route.
Meanwhile, the Guards' naval commander said this week that vessels that deactivate their navigation systems would be considered hostile.
Two different warnings.
Ships face risk whether they are seen or not.
Lever seven.
Naval Facilitation..
The US doesn't describe most of this as classic escorts.
The words are "assisted" and "coordinated protection." Ships can get route guidance from a US Navy cell, and according to JMIC, that coordination is voluntary.
Most of it runs along a southern route hugging the coast of Oman.
At the same time, CENTCOM describes a US blockade of ships linked to Iranian ports.
JMIC, citing CENTCOM figures, says 135 vessels had been redirected and four disabled as of October 10th and 11th.
So both sides run a control system.
Iran runs permission on the northern lane.
The US runs guidance on the southern lane, plus what CENTCOM describes as a blockade.
UKMTO says most ships broadcasting AIS still use Iran's route.
It also cites a ratio of about five to one, which its report doesn't fully explain.
The strait is effectively two lanes with two rulebooks.
Part five.
Ships Versus Barrels.
Here's a wrinkle that explains some of the confusion.
Ship counts are low.
But oil volumes aren't as low as ship counts would suggest.

The IEA says September's increase, to about 10.9 million barrels a day, was helped by robust ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, where cargo moves from one tanker to another outside the strait.
It also reports that pipelines bypassing the strait raised bypass exports to 5.6 million barrels a day.
And Kpler told AFP that most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore.
And daily numbers swing wildly.
Kpler data cited by Al Jazeera shows nearly 20.8 million barrels crossing on October 8th, and only 2.9 million on October 11th.
CENTCOM, for its part, said US forces helped Gulf partners ship more than 19 million barrels on Monday, October 12th.
Those numbers use different definitions and different time windows, which is why weekly averages are more reliable than any single day.
That is one reading of why low ship counts and large barrel numbers can appear in the same news cycle.
Part six.
So What Does "Closed" Mean?.
Let's go back to the question.
There are three ways to be closed.
Legally closed.
Does anyone have the authority to shut it?
That's disputed.
JMIC said in July that no single nation controls the strait.
Iran says it can, as a matter of security.
Physically closed.
Can a ship get through?
Yes.
Some do, every day: roughly 30 a day by the US count, a dozen or fewer by independent trackers.
None of the sources used here reports zero.
Commercially closed.
Will ordinary shipowners send ordinary cargoes at ordinary cost?
On that test, UKMTO puts traffic about 70 percent below pre-war levels.
JMIC's three anchorage counts add up to roughly 430 ships at anchor off the UAE and Oman.
And by the IEA's figures, September's oil flows were a little over half of the pre-war level.
In this video's reading, Iran's statement leans on that third definition, and on a claim to authority.
The US statement leans on the second, and on its ability to help ships through.
They also make competing claims about who controls the strait.
A strait doesn't close like a door.
It closes like a market: through fear, price and permission.
And right now, neither side's declaration alone controls all three.
What should you watch?
The weekly UKMTO overview, published on Fridays.
JMIC's threat level.
War-risk insurance quotes.
The IEA's monthly report.
And diplomacy.
On October 8th, President Trump said on social media that the US would not attack Iran before the November 3rd midterm elections, and that his team was having productive discussions with Iran.
Iran's foreign minister said Tehran expected to give a formal reply to a US counterproposal within days.
As of October 18th, no agreement had been announced in the sources used here.
Everything in this video reflects information available as of October 18th, 2026.
This situation is changing day by day.
Sources for every figure are in the description.
